facts.claim: Chapter 'Disappearing Act: How to Escape the Office'. Ferriss introduces Sherwood and Johanna earlier as worked case studies ('Let's use two people, Sherwood and Johanna'); the remote-work section returns to Sherwood under the heading 'Trading Bosses for Beer: An Oktoberfest Case Study'.

Sherwood is a mechanical engineer who sells French sailor shirts on the side; after cutting time-wasters he produces twice as many designs in half the time. He has moved about 80% of communication with his boss to e-mail and 20% to phone and deliberately holds back some productivity to show a jump later.

Five steps starting July 12 in the slow season, lasting about two months, ending with two weeks at Oktoberfest in Munich: 1 increase investment (asks the company to pay for a four-week industrial design class), 2 prove output offsite, 3 prepare quantifiable benefit, 4 propose a revocable trial, 5 expand remote time.

Step 2: he calls in sick on Tuesday and Wednesday, doubles output, leaves an e-mail trail, and uses a free trial of GoToMyPC to run the CAD software licensed on his office desktop. Result: three more designs per day than his average and three extra billable hours in total.

Step 4: around 3 p.m. on a relaxed Thursday he knocks on boss Bill's door, asks for 'two minutes', and proposes working from home Mondays and Tuesdays for a two-week trial that Bill can veto any time. He asked for two days so he could fall back to one if refused; Bill agrees: 'it's just a test'.

Step 5: he makes remote days his most productive, brings a bullet-point page of results, asks for four days remote for another two weeks, ready to settle for three. Bill worries he is on his way out and that everyone will want the same; Sherwood answers that only people who show higher productivity should get it. Bill agrees: 'don't go blabbing about it.'

On September 19 he asks for a two-week full-time remote trial while visiting relatives, timing it during a project that needs him, prepared to quit; the boss agrees. Ferriss: getting what you want often depends more on when you ask than how. Sherwood buys a $524 round-trip ticket to Munich.

Ferriss's two aims: show the business benefit of remote work and make it too costly to refuse. Two days instead of five because it is less for management to accept and lets him rehearse remote work first.
Same chapter opens with a real case: Dave Camarillo of HP, who worked from China for 30 days without telling anyone.

rejected.claim: 'Ferriss tells the story of a real client'
rejected.reason: Sherwood is the book's illustrative case study, not presented as a real client

rejected.claim: Worked two months from Portugal; arrangement made permanent
rejected.reason: Book: Munich, Oktoberfest, two weeks; no Portugal, no 'permanent'

rejected.claim: Proposal line 'I can work from Europe for two months; if performance drops I'll come back'
'Many limits are just boundaries never asked about' as Ferriss's quote

1296.note: Center (step-by-step remote negotiation) is in the book; rebuilt on Sherwood's actual steps, clearly framed as the book's worked example. Calling in sick is the book's tactic and is reported, not endorsed.
